My Experience at Collective Artists Network (Galleri5)

I recently got laid off from Collective Artists Networks Galleri5 division, just five months into my one-year contract. But what disappointed me wasnt just the layoff. It was everything that happened before it. I joined on April 13 as an AI + 3D Generalist.
 During hiring, HR mentioned multiple upcoming projects, possible contract extensions, and working hours of Monday–Friday, 10 AM–6:30 PM, with Saturdays as WFH if required.

On my very first day, I learned that Saturdays werent off. Initially, I was assigned to Krishna, while another team worked on Hanuman. Some newly hired artists remained unassigned for weeks, and a few were terminated before even starting project work so why were they even hired. In June, our entire Krishna team was shifted to Hanuman due to production deadlines, yet some unassigned artists still werent included and were eventually laid off. Why hire artists if there isnt enough work for them, especially when another team is overloaded? We worked 10–12+ hours daily, Monday through Saturday, with Sunday work also expected, without additional monetary compensation for my extra hours. Instead, we were promised two weeks of compensatory leave.Despite repeated layoffs creating constant job insecurity, we continued giving our best to the project. By mid-August, the films first pass was completed. I scheduled my promised leave for September 7–18. Before leaving, a team lead even offered me another project after my return.But during that very leave, HR called to inform me I was being terminated due to downsizing. HR initially asked me to resign voluntarily, which I refused since the decision wasnt mine. I received my termination letter on September 16.When I returned my laptop, the team lead told me he hadnt known about my termination and had requested management to retain me for his project, but the decision was already processed.If another team needed my skills, why wasnt that considered before terminating me?

Even my full-and-final settlement arrived on October 8, later than the seven-working-day timeline communicated by HR.

I understand my contract allowed early termination, and downsizing sometimes happens. But recruitment promises that dont match reality, poor resource management, excessive working hours, and constant job insecurity shouldnt be normalized.Artists are expected to treat projects as their own, sacrifice weekends, and give everything to meet deadlines. But once the work is completed, are those same artists simply an expense to be cut?Im sharing my experience because artists deserve transparency, fair working conditions, and respect.

Before approving another headcount request, I would ask five questions.

When a business unit asks for 20 new hires, 9 out of 10 times they don't have a hiring problem. They have a #workforceplanningproblem.

#Hiring is the most expensive reflex to a capacity crunch. As #HR leaders navigating AI adoption and shifting skill demands, our job isn't to fill seats it's to architect capability.

Before posting a single JD, run this filter:
#CriticalRole RealityCheck: Does this deliver core competitive advantage, or is it operational drift?

#DemandForecastStressTest: Is this volume spike durable for 18 months, or a 90-day seasonal backlog?

#ProductivityBaseline: Have we integrated GenAI and streamlined broken handoffs, or are we just throwing headcount at bad process design?

#SkillsInventory: What adjacent talent already sits inside our teams, ready for a 6-week reskill or internal move?

#Build vs. #BuyEconomics: Can we contract the peak, automate the workflow, and build the critical core internally?

Growth doesn't come from aggressive hiring. It comes from disciplined workforce allocation.

What’s the first question you ask before signing off on headcount?

My story of 4 jobs landed without email, AI, LinkedIn OR responding to postings (back then it was ads in the paper) . . . in both strong and rough job markets. 

JOB #1: 

I spoke with friends who landed roles and was pointed to a temp-to-perm agency, where I landed a permanent role at an Association in Washington, DC.

TAKEAWAY LESSON: Consider contract or fractional roles. 

JOB #2: 

I told friends I was unhappy with Job #1, and my friend at the World Bank told me about a small consulting firm she worked with that was hiring . After reaching out with her referral and getting an interview, I was hired. 

TAKEAWAY LESSON: Don't overlook small companies or boutique firms. 

JOB #3: 

With plans to relocate and make a career pivot after earning my master's in a graduate social work program, I reached out to current and former professors and asked if they knew any colleagues in my new city. One did. 

I left a voicemail asking if we could speak, which we did. She gave me a few names, and I rinsed and repeated to land a role doing social work case management for a Medicaid home health hospice program. 

TAKEAWAY LESSON: Tap into warm but second-string contacts in your network. 

JOB #4: 

I told anyone I came in contact with that I was looking to pivot AGAIN (this time back to corporate from social work). I shared with them what I was good at (writing and listening to people) and the type of role I was targeting.

An alum a few years ahead of me introduced me to a recruiter at a growing financial services company. He said I'd be great for a newly created and as-yet-unpublished role managing a small Communications and Training team at one of their de novo startups. 

I went through a series of interviews and an assessment before I was offered and accepted the role.

TAKEAWAY LESSON: The more targeted the ask, the greater the help.

REST, GraphQL, SOAP… choosing an API isn't just about knowing the names. It's about understanding what your system actually needs. 👇

Think about the applications you use every day:
🌦️ A weather app fetching live data
🔐 A website handling login requests
🏦 A banking platform processing transactions
📊 A dashboard retrieving data from multiple services
🤝 Two companies connecting their systems

All of these can involve APIs, but the way they communicate can be very different.
Here's a quick breakdown of the types shown in this visual:
🔹 REST APIs - Common for web apps, product data, and authentication.
🔹 SOAP APIs - Often used in enterprise environments where strict contracts and established integration standards matter.
🔹 GraphQL APIs - Useful when clients need flexibility in choosing exactly which data they want.
🔹 Internal APIs - Connect services within an application or organization, such as a frontend, backend, and database layer.
🔹 Partner APIs - Enable integrations with external businesses, payment providers, booking platforms, and other services.
🔹 Data-Sharing APIs - Allow systems to exchange information across platforms, such as logistics, finance, or healthcare data.

One important thing to remember: these categories aren't all mutually exclusive. REST, SOAP, and GraphQL describe API approaches, while internal, partner, and data-sharing APIs describe how or where APIs are used.

When designing a system, the better questions are:
→ Who will consume the API?
→ What data needs to be exchanged?
→ How should authentication and security work?
→ What performance, reliability, and compatibility requirements exist?
Understanding these trade-offs is what helps you move beyond simply using APIs to designing better backend systems.

15+ CLM implementations in, the problem I see most isn't the platform.

It's the gap between the contract system and the tools people already work in.

Legal lives in the CLM. Everyone else lives in Jira, SharePoint and Salesforce. So requests arrive by email, someone retypes a record ID, and the contract stalls at a handoff nobody owns.

Three things I've built to close that gap:

• An Atlassian Forge app that creates ContractPodAI (Leah) contract requests from inside a Jira issue and keeps stage and document links in sync, so users never type a request ID
• Jira webhooks that open a legal review ticket automatically when a contract deviates from policy
• A SharePoint integration on ContractPodAI's REST API that removes manual version  generation

None of it is exotic. It's REST APIs and careful UAT. But it's the difference between a CLM that's configured and a CLM that's used.

I'm a CLM Functional Consultant at Integreon, working across ContractPodAI (Leah AI), Ironclad, DocuSign CLM and Zoho CLM.

If you run CLM at your company, where do your contracts stall: the platform, or the handoffs around it?

The holiday hiring freeze is here 📉

US employers announced the fewest September seasonal hiring plans since 2011 — down 23% from last year, according to Challenger data reported this week. The usual year-end hiring surge isn't coming.

My take: a hiring freeze doesn't mean careers freeze. It means the old playbook stops working.

When employers pull back, the people who keep growing do three things:

→ Skill up while the market is quiet. The AI tools reshaping your industry won't wait for hiring to recover.
→ Earn while you search. Freelance, contract, project work — income now, portfolio later.
→ Go public with your expertise. A visible portfolio beats a stack of applications every time.

Downturns don't reward the most anxious applicant. They reward the most adaptable professional.

Question for you: if hiring stayed frozen for 6 months, what would you build or learn with that time? 👇

Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) plans to ensure that around 80% of its future new hires have digital and artificial intelligence skills, as the IT services company expands its AI business and looks to improve profitability. Chief Operating Officer Arathi Subramanian  shared the hiring outlook in an interview with PTI.

The company added 4,500 employees in the September quarter, of whom 25% to 30% had specialised AI skills, while around 80% had what Subramanian described as “new-age” skills. She said TCS expects this hiring mix to continue, adding that the required talent is available in the market.

AI-led work accounted for 10% of TCS’ revenue in the quarter ended September 2026. Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director K Krithivasan said a growing contribution from AI projects could support margin expansion as these engagements increase in volume.

TCS is also continuing to invest in specialised talent, partnerships and acquisitions. Krithivasan said professionals willing to learn new skills can benefit from their existing understanding of technology and industry domains, suggesting that AI-driven changes in the workforce will not necessarily favour fresh graduates over experienced engineers.

The company said customers are often starting with AI projects in specific business areas before expanding them after seeing results. While TCS is cautious about classifying deals as AI-led, Krithivasan said some element of AI is now involved in virtually all the company’s work. Its second-quarter total contract value stood at $9.6 billion.

The strategy comes as IT services companies face pressure to adapt their delivery models to AI, which can improve productivity but also challenge traditional billing models. TCS reported an operating margin of 24% for the September quarter and annualised AI revenue of $3.1 billion.

Procurement Professionals over 40 years of age are Facing difficulties in landing new jobs, here is why:

Procurement Professionals can inbox their CV for a Free Review And Feedback.

1. Age and Salary Expectation Bias: Some employers may hesitate to recruit experienced procurement professionals due to assumptions about salary expectations, adaptability, or willingness to work in positions with narrower purchasing responsibilities.

2. AI and Automation Adaptability Bias: Some employers assume experienced procurement professionals may struggle to adapt to e-procurement platforms, AI-powered sourcing tools, automated purchasing workflows, and emerging supply chain technologies, overlooking their actual capabilities.

3. Unfamiliarity with Modern CV Requirements: After years in procurement, you may not know what today's HR professionals and hiring managers expect to see in a CV, how they assess candidates, or which procurement achievements deserve priority.

4. Overemphasis on Older Experience: Focus on your most recent 10 years. Summarise earlier positions instead of detailing every purchasing responsibility, keeping attention on your current procurement capabilities and strategic sourcing experience.

5. Responsibilities Instead of Achievements: Listing routine purchase orders, supplier coordination, and quotation comparisons without demonstrating cost savings, supplier performance improvements, procurement efficiency, or contract value optimisation weakens your profile.

6. Limited Procurement Software Visibility: Employers may look for proficiency in SAP Ariba, Oracle Procurement, Coupa, Microsoft Dynamics, ERP systems, or other role-specific sourcing platforms. Your CV must reflect the tools you genuinely use.

7. Changing Procurement and Compliance Requirements: Updated procurement policies, supplier due diligence requirements, contract regulations, sustainability standards, and public or private sector compliance frameworks can influence hiring decisions.

8. Weak Analytical and Digital Skills: Limited evidence of expertise in spend analysis, demand forecasting, supplier risk assessment, advanced Excel, procurement dashboards, or automated purchasing reports may affect competitiveness for certain roles.
